items.title: Was Benjamin Franklin the original wellness bro? I lived like him for a day to find out
items.summary:
Before online influencers existed, the founding father published an annual wellness pamphlet. I followed his 13 virtues he found necessary for a good life

Benjamin Franklin doesn’t get enough credit. Yes, he was a founding father of the United States; he invented the lightning rod and his face is printed on $100 bills. But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing.

Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.”

items.title: Let’s hear it for the leftwing echo chamber | Zoe Williams
items.summary:
By chance, I found myself committed to a debate with people whose views I share. It was an eye-opening experience

I was on a panel recently in a church – St Luke’s in Battersea, south London – about the future of the welfare state, except the other panellists booked to speak on the right of politics were unwell and couldn’t come. And so we ended up with an entirely leftwing panel (albeit different shades of the left).

Puckishly, I suggested that I would split my six minutes of allocated speaking time and do three on what the rightwing panellists would have said, had they appeared, and then three on why they are wrong. But I couldn’t get the arguments right. I know they think the current welfare bill is – between our ageing population, our Neets and our dated expectations about what a decent life looks like and whose job it is to ensure you have one – “unsustainable”. I just couldn’t summon the right mix of tough-minded realism and benign resignation to other people’s misery. It wouldn’t come out of my mouth.

items.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee

These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

items.title: Massachusetts sues Trump admin to stop ICE's courthouse arrests: 'Unnecessary fear'
items.summary:
Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration on Monday to block Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from carrying out civil arrests in the state's courthouses, arguing that such arrests without judicial warrants are illegal under state law.

The lawsuit filed by Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell challenges a 2025 ICE directive that authorizes agents to conduct civil arrests in or near state courthouses without judicial warrants, which she says violates the PROTECT Act, a new state law passed ​by the Democratic-led legislature that prohibits civil immigration arrests in state courthouses without judicial warrants. The courthouse protections took effect Nov. 3.

Campbell said the ICE directive interferes with the state's authority to operate its judicial system, disrupts court proceedings, undermines constitutional principles and public safety and spreads fear, chaos and confusion.

"The Massachusetts PROTECT Act makes it illegal for ICE to conduct civil arrests in our courthouses without a judicial warrant. ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable," Campbell said in a statement.

items.title: Unsealed warrant documents for Ilhan Omar's DC home raid reveal decades-long scope of investigation
items.summary:
Heavily redacted versions of documents used to justify a search warrant and raid on the Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., were released to the public Monday evening.

Despite the level of redaction, the documents provide more insight into the scope of the investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman. 

In an ex parte brief in support of an affidavit for a search warrant, federal prosecutors say they're searching for all "records and information that constitute fruits, contraband, evidence, and instrumentalities of violations of [redacted], those violations involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present (the 'Target Offenses)."

While accounts vary, even from the congresswoman herself, Omar was born in 1981 or 1982. She does not have a birth certificate. She came to the United States in 1995 with her father. Fox News Digital confirmed just after the Oct. 12 raid of her home, that investigators were looking into alleged immigration fraud, potentially related to how Omar and her father filled out her immigration paperwork. 

In another document, arguing that the court mischaracterized the government's arguments in ex parte proceedings, prosecutors make it clear that the investigation into Omar spans decades. 

"The United States believes that ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades— beginning long before she was ever in Congress," the document says.…

items.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
items.summary:
On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing

During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union.

Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels.

The Maybot spent three years saying nothing more intelligent than “Brexit means Brexit”. Boris lied through his teeth to get his deal over the line. And as for Rishi? It’s hard to think of anything he achieved.

All of which makes life tricky for Kemi Badenoch. Because in an ideal world, Kemi would rather we all forgot about Brexit entirely. Not because it is going so well, but because it isn’t. items.summary:
The government, as well as the inspectorate, must take responsibility for reforms that have not worked out

The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.

Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments. items.title: How did Republicans lose so badly in North Carolina?
items.summary:
Republicans suffered sweeping losses across the US in the midterm elections, but perhaps nowhere as large as here

Republicans suffered sweeping losses across the country in the midterm elections, but perhaps nowhere as large as North Carolina.

Democrats flipped a US Senate seat for the first time since 2008, as well as five House seats, one of which Cook Political Report had rated “solid” Republican, and four others considered “likely” Republican. Democrats also held power in the state’s first district, which Republicans had targeted in a redistricting effort.

Since entering Downing Street, raising “growth in every postcode” has been the prime minister’s rallying cry, as he bids to close the gaping chasm in living standards between the richest and poorest areas of the country. But as the war in the Middle East intensifies, the task of spreading prosperity far and wide has only become more difficult.

items.title: Trump inspired a blue revolution. Can Democrats meet the moment? | Dana R Fisher
items.summary:
Political participation – in meetings, boycotts and demonstrations – has increased since Trump took office. It’s time for change

Over the past two years, Americans have watched as the Trump administration enacted Project 2025 and the US has descended into a state of lawless authoritarianism. Instead of sinking into a state of paralysis, though, Americans rose up to push back against the attacks, including limitations of voting rights and manipulations of political power through the gerrymandering of congressional districts.

Donald Trump’s actions motivated resistance in the streets in the form of large-scale public demonstrations, along with more localized mobilizations against ICE and the occupation of American cities. On 3 November, the collective response manifested as resistance at the ballot box.
